rect.title: <b>MCCCOMM111 The Art of Rhetorical Communication</b><br>Teaches how to craft persuasive messages, influence opinions, inspire action and<br>connect people. Draws on historical communicators from Aristotle to Barack Obama<br>and applies stylistic techniques to students’ own writing and speaking.

<b>MCCCOMM112 Dutch</b><br>This course aims to develop basic skills and strategies necessary to<br>successfully handle uncomplicated oral and written communication in Dutch<br>in a variety of social situations that you may encounter in daily life in<br>the Netherlands. The emphasis in the course will be on speaking in Dutch in<br>day-to-day situations on the one hand and understanding Dutch culture on the<br>other hand. At the end of the course students can orally express and write<br>about themselves in Dutch, who they are, describe their family background, and<br>interact with others in a simple way.

<b>MCCCOMM211 Style & Meaning</b><br>Explores how linguistic choices inform meaning and interpretation in literary<br>and non-fiction contexts. Introduces theoretical frameworks for close reading<br>and addresses power dynamics, obligation, uncertainty and ideological undertones<br>in language.

<b>MCCCOMM212 Communicating the Climate Crisis</b><br>Examines how the climate crisis is communicated and contested. Analyzes texts,<br>films, exhibitions, protest art, slogans and social media alongside theory<br>and case studies, teaching students to dissect arguments and culminating in a<br>project where students enter the debate.

<b>MCCCOMM213 Rhetoric in Action</b><br>Develops persuasive speaking skills by applying rhetorical theory in the<br>real world. Students work with local primary school children, building<br>public-speaking skills and empowering them to find their voices.

<b>MCCCOMM311 Persuasive Communication</b><br>Explores ethical persuasion and climate communication. Students learn persuasive<br>communication models and frameworks and collaborate with climate scientists at<br>the Delta Climate Centre to produce sustainability messaging on water, food and<br>energy.

<b>MCCCOMM312 Creative Communication Laboratory</b><br>Explores meaning-making through creative expression. Students study and practice<br>poetic forms, experiment with sonic poetry, performance and other unconventional<br>forms of communication, engage with theoretical texts and produce their own<br>creative work.

<b>MCCHEAM111 Introduction to Western Art History</b><br>Provides an introduction to Western art history, tracing major artistic<br>movements from the late Middle Ages to the present. Through close study of<br>key paintings and their makers, students gain insight into evolving styles,<br>techniques and cultural influences.

<b>MCCHEAM112 Introduction to World Archaeology</b><br>Explores ancient craft production from around the world. Examines how making<br>objects shaped human development and how ancient solutions can inform modern<br>sustainability.

<b>MCCHEAM211 African Art & Heritage</b><br>Examines the artistic, historical and ethical dimensions of African art.<br>Highlights distinct forms and cultural significance, considers influence<br>on Western modernism and addresses looting, colonial-era acquisitions and<br>repatriation efforts.

<b>MCCHEAM212 Renaissance Italy & Global Mediterranean</b><br>This course examines the painting, sculpture, and architecture of Renaissance<br>Italy and the extensive artistic connections that linked the Italian peninsula<br>to other regions of the world. By exploring a range of geographical contexts,<br>from the Islamic courts of the Eastern Mediterranean and the commercial routes<br>connecting Europe, Asia, and Africa to the newly encountered territories of<br>the Americas, students will examine how trade, colonization, and cross-cultural<br>exchange shaped the production and meaning of Renaissance art.

<b>MCCHEAM213 Greek Archaeology</b><br>The invention of democracy in classical Greece changed the nature of community<br>decision-making, perhaps forever. This process is reflected in the material<br>culture of the period. By examining the archaeology of community & democracy in<br>early-democratic Greece, this course goes in search of ancient lessons for the<br>modern world.

<b>MCCHEAM312 Modern Art & Modern Museums</b><br>Examines debates on modern art through various themes. Focuses on the<br>relationship between art and its presentation in museums and exhibitions,<br>exploring curatorial practices and exhibition strategies.

<b>MCCHEAM315 Heritage & Ancient Democracy</b><br>In the modern world democracy is associated with participation, rationality and<br>freedom. In this course, we go back to the roots of democracy in ancient Greece,<br>when to a modern observer, it was not very democratic at all: foreigners, slaves<br>and women were excluded from elections and political decision-making. Even so,<br>the inclusion of all classes, also the poor, in politics was after antiquity<br>not achieved until the mid-nineteenth century. Ancient commentators criticised<br>Athenian democracy for being too extreme just because of this broad inclusion.<br>They argued that many were too uneducated, too emotional, and too irrational to<br>see through the cheap play on emotions by demagogues and would-be tyrants. This<br>course investigates how Athenian democracy was built, how it was intertwined<br>with myth and religion, and expressed in art, literature and architecture. It<br>traces the loci of democracy in archaeology, and analyses its temporary collapse<br>in the crisis of the late fifth century BC. Most importantly, we put ourselves<br>in our socio-political ancestors’ shoes by engaging in a simulation of the<br>Athenian assembly, in which we have to make decisions that will change our lives<br>forever. In doing so, we use the ancient heritage of democracy for an experiment<br>in applied sociology – to not only understand, but to feel the meaning of<br>political decision-making.

<b>MCCHEAM316 Writing Art's Histories</b><br>This course examines the history of art history as an academic discipline,<br>tracing how scholars have understood and interpreted art from the sixteenth<br>century to the present. Through critical readings of influential texts by<br>figures such as Aby Warburg, Erwin Panofsky, Ernst Gombrich, Michel Foucault,<br>and Jacques Derrida, students explore the major ideas and methodologies that<br>have shaped the field. Topics include art and history, aesthetics, meaning and<br>interpretation, authorship and identity, and the challenges of art history in a<br>globalized world.

<b>MCCLITR111 Introduction to Literary Studies</b><br>Introduces what literature is, why we read it and how to interpret it. Covers<br>fiction, poetry, drama, non‑fiction and film narration, exploring various<br>literary forms and genres such as graphic narratives and romance novels.

<b>MCCLITR112 Great Literary Works</b><br>Provides a chronological overview of literature from the epic of Gilgamesh to<br>post‑modernity. Reads literary and critical texts that explore human experience<br>and teaches how to approach literature’s ambiguities and trace themes across<br>ages.

<b>MCCLITR211 World Myth & Literature</b><br>Investigates myths from around the world—from Gilgamesh to the Ramayana, Greek<br>and Norse myths. Explores how myths underpin literature and connects them to<br>contemporary global cultures.

<b>MCCLITR212 Life & Travel Writing</b><br>Examines autobiographical and travel writing. Explores how individuals write<br>about self, identity and bodily experience; discusses tropes and models used to<br>represent human experience; and considers memory and imagination in writing.

<b>MCCLITR311 Film & Text</b><br>Studies complex links between literary and film narratives. Analyzes<br>formal aspects of both media, discusses adaptation, intertextuality, viewer<br>participation and narrative dynamics, and allows students to research topics<br>like literature‑to‑film adaptation and cross‑cultural themes.

<b>MCCLITR312 Perspectives on Literary Meaning</b><br>Examines how different perspectives—humanist, feminist, Marxist, cultural<br>minority and psychoanalytic—affect reading and interpretation. Students<br>undertake a research project applying selected perspectives to texts.

<b>MCCMEDI111 Introduction to Film & Media</b><br>Introduces film and media as systems of meaning and cultural production.<br>Examines how images, narratives and technologies shape perception, identity<br>and power; covers film storytelling, representation and genres; and develops<br>critical engagement skills.

<b>MCCMEDI112 Media Archaeology</b><br>Explores media technologies before digital culture. Studies cassette tapes,<br>typewriters and early printing as material objects that carry meaning; includes<br>hands‑on experiments; no technical background required.

<b>MCCMEDI211 From T.V. to TikTok</b><br>Explores how media shape attitudes and provide answers through examples from TV<br>and TikTok. Examines messages that teach fear, pity, admiration and allyship.

<b>MCCMEDI212 Media & the Environment</b><br>Examines representation of environmental concerns through visual culture.<br>Explores the Anthropocene, animal representation, deep time, biocentrism,<br>contested nature, indigenous and postcolonial media; analyzes how media shape<br>environmental understanding; and includes a paper or media project.

<b>MCCMEDI311 Media & Race</b><br>Investigates storytelling and power in relation to race. Examines Afrofuturism<br>and systemic racism and guides students in creating podcasts that explore links<br>between past and present.

<b>MCCMEDI312 The Documentary</b><br>Introduces development of the documentary form. Students write a theoretical<br>paper and produce a short documentary film, fostering understanding of<br>documentary diversity and providing analytical tools for documentary study.
No GATE
